title: Chapter 94 – Provisional
html:
[Azure Cloud Sect – Lin Jian]

The top of the emergency stair is a wall with a hole in it, and the hole is very small.

Jian reaches it on his hands and knees. His legs gave out at step two hundred and ninety, and he has crawled the rest, pulling himself up by the stone lip of each tread with one numb hand and one that shakes. The light that spills down from above is gray and cold. It smells of snow, of pine pitch, of ten thousand cooking fires, and he breathes it in until his lungs hurt.

Out, says Pebble, from inside his tunic. Out out out.

"I know."

The wall in front of him is the same black stone as the one that sealed him in. He puts his palm on it. The Seal gives a weak pulse, a bruised and unwilling one, and under his hand the stone goes warm and then soft, and then folds back on itself in dark petals, one after another, with a sound like a very large book being opened.

Daylight comes in like a blow.

He stumbles forward into it, blind, and a hand takes him under the arm before he falls. The hand is old and dry and strong. It smells of ink and lamp oil.

"Easy," says Elder Qin Hao.

* * *

The first thing he sees, once his eyes stop streaming, is the face of the man who is holding him up.

Qin Hao has aged. It is not the kind of aging that shows in the skin. His beard is as neat as ever and his robe is clean. It is something behind the eyes, a tightness, the look of a man who has gone three days without sleep and then been given something to carry. His grip on Jian's arm is firm. The other hand, Jian notices, is resting on the black stone beside the doorway as if it has been there all night.

"You are alive," the Elder says.

"Yes, Elder."

"You are not the same as when you went in."

Jian looks down at himself. The tunic is gray with dust. His left arm hangs heavy from the shoulder. He has no CE and a Seal that aches in time with his breath, and somewhere in the cold dark under his ribs there is a seed the size of a pea that was not there three days ago, humming softly to itself. The Door in Winter. He has told himself he will not think of it until he is somewhere safe.

"I have been fasting, Elder," he says. "It makes a man thin."

Something moves in Qin Hao's face. It is not quite a smile.

"Three days," the Elder says quietly. "You have not been seen. You have not been heard. Your family has sat at the foot of this stair since the dawn after you went in. The council is tied. I have given my name as surety that you are no harm. You will walk down this slope in front of two hundred disciples, and when you are asked what you saw, you will say as little as you can and still be truthful."

"Yes, Elder."

"And you will not faint."

"I will try not to."

"That is all I ask." The Elder lets go of his arm. "Walk."

* * *

The slope below the fortieth landing is white with new snow.

They have kept a path clear down the center, a trench a body wide, and on either side of it the disciples stand shoulder to shoulder in the gray and silver of Enforcement and the plain gray of the Outer Court. He sees faces he knows. The Reed Courtyard cook, with her hands wrapped in her apron. A big Terrace Nine boy who once shared a bowl with him in the rain. Two Gate guards who looked at his token and said nothing, a year ago. A hundred and some others who look at him, now, with an expression he has not seen on any of them before.

Not fear. Not quite. It is the way people look at a river that has changed its course.

He walks the path. Each step is a decision. The snow squeaks under his boots. Qin Hao walks half a pace behind and to the left, where a guard walks, and does not touch him again.

At the foot of the stair three people stand up.

His father reaches him first. Lin Wenyuan has not run in twenty years, and he does not run now, but his stride is not quite a stride, and when he gets close he stops short, as if he has forgotten what comes next. His face is thin. His hair has more gray in it than Jian remembers. For a moment he only looks.

Then he puts a hand on Jian's shoulder, and the hand is trembling.

"You are very thin," says Lin Wenyuan.

"I was told that."

"You will eat."

"Yes, Father."

His mother does not speak at all. Su Qinghe comes into his arms with her head against his collarbone, and he feels the whole length of her shaking, small, hard, silent. She holds him the way she held him when he was a boy with a fever, with both arms and her whole weight. Over her head, Feng stands very straight with his fists at his sides, tall and sun-dark and furious, and when their eyes meet his brother says only, in a rough voice:

"Idiot."

"I know."

"Three days."

"I know."

"I had a wedge," says Feng. "I would have used it."

"I know that too."

Pebble pokes its snout out of his collar and sneezes. Qinghe makes a sound halfway between a laugh and a sob. Feng closes his eyes for a moment, and opens them, and for the first time in three days looks his age.

* * *

The hearing is held on the stair, in the open, because no one has been able to agree on a room.

The Arbiter comes down from the Law Pavilion in a plain black robe, his staff across his arm, and takes the third step above the snow. The Elders gather behind him. Jian sees Mu, stern and gray, with his hands behind his back. Zhou, who will not meet anyone's eye. Elder Ye of the Sutra Hall, small and upright, her gray braid over her shoulder, who looks at him as a scholar looks at a page. And Bai, last, with a plum in each hand and a faint smell of herbs, who nods at him, once, as one nods to a patient.

"Disciple Lin Jian, token 0417," says Shen Wuye. "Do you stand for yourself?"

"I do, Arbiter."

"The floor was tied on the matter of your standing. A tie holds while the cause of the vote continues." The Arbiter taps his staff on the stair. "The cause has ceased. The door is open. By Article twelve, the matter now falls to the Guard's surety, which was lodged and not withdrawn." He looks around the ring. "The Guard's stake stands. The disciple is named Gate Bearer, provisional, under the Guard's name."

A murmur goes through the crowd, and dies at once.

"The provisional bearer is not owned by the Sect, nor held by it. He is studied, and he is answerable. His standing will be reviewed at the winter solstice of the year after next. Until then he is moved from the Outer Court to the Inner Court, on probation, under the supervision of an Elder of the floor." The staff turns. "The Sutra Hall has asked for him. Elder Ye?"

"The Sutra Hall accepts," says Ye, in a clear thin voice.

"Elder Mu."

Mu inclines his head a fraction. "The Law notes the arrangement. The Law does not approve it." He pauses, and his gaze rests on Jian, and it is not hostile. It is the look of a man holding a very old and very sharp tool, and wondering what it is for. "The Law will watch."

"Then it is so recorded."

The Arbiter strikes his staff on the stair a second time, and the sound runs out over the snow like a bell.

Provisional. Jian lets the word settle. It is a rope, thrown to a man who was drowning, and it is also a leash. He has a ring in his nose now, and the one holding it has an interest in how he moves.

* * *

"Eat," says Bai.

The Pill Hall smells of boiled roots and smoke. It is a low, wide building with a hundred small furnaces, and the old Elder's spare cot stands in an alcove behind a screen, where the warmth from the main hearth reaches it through a hole in the wall. Jian sits on the edge of it with a bowl of barley porridge steaming in his hands. His fingers do not feel like his own.

He eats. It is the best thing he has ever tasted.

"Slowly," says Bai. "You will be sick."

"Yes, Elder."

"Stop saying yes, Elder. You will be saying it to Ye for the next two years. You can say something else to me." The stout old man drops onto a stool, wheezing, and unwraps a plum from a twist of paper. "You are no longer my apprentice. The Sutra Hall has you in the Inner Court, and an Inner disciple does not mix powder for a Pill Hall Elder. That is the Rule. I am sorry for it."

"Rank One does not leave me."

"It does not. The favor you owe me does not either." Bai bites the plum and chews with relish. "A night in the Garden when your trust runs out. I have not forgotten and neither have you. But the Inner Court will give you better teachers than I am, and a wider library, and a great many people who would like to find out what you are."

"That is what concerns me, Elder."

"It should." Bai's small eyes do not leave him. "Show me your hand."

Jian puts down the spoon and offers his right. Bai takes his wrist between two thick fingers, and the room goes very quiet.

"Hm," says the Elder.

He holds it for a count of twenty. Jian does not breathe. He has no Veil, and he has no reserve to throw one up, and he knows what a Pill Hall Elder can read in a pulse. The Foundation base is there under his ribs like a lamp in a window. The Seal is a second heart. The seed is a third.

"Hm," says Bai again, and lets him go.

"Elder?"

"I have felt nothing," says Bai, "that I did not feel the day Mirror read you QR nine. Mind that I say it. A man with sharp senses might say otherwise. I am an old man with a poor sense of smell." He chews, swallows, picks a fiber from his teeth. "Be careful of Ye. She is not cruel. She is thorough. There is a difference, and it is not always to the advantage of the thing being studied."

"I will remember."

"And finish the porridge. I did not boil it for fun."

* * *

His family is allowed an hour.

The Arbiter grants it at the foot of the stair, with a brisk wave of his staff and a look at the sky, and the Enforcement disciples move back a decent distance. They sit on a stone bench in the lee of the wall, out of the wind, and his mother puts a hot flask in his hands. Jian drinks. It is ginger and honey and something bitter, and it goes down like a fire.

"You will not tell us what you saw," says Wenyuan. It is not a question.

"I will tell you what I can. There is a room. It is old. It holds records, and a bench for the Founder's work. I learned something there. I paid for it." He rolls the flask between his palms. "That is all I can say to you now, and it is more than I can say to anyone else."

"Is it dangerous?"

"Yes."

"Is it worth it?"

He thinks of the name on the panel, of the line in the register, of the slip of white paper he has not yet seen. "I do not know yet."

Wenyuan nods slowly, as if this is the best answer he could have hoped for.

"Then I will give you what we have," he says, "and you may do with it as you see fit. The Garden is quiet. The Court inspector came last week and found no fault. Zhong's ledger shows the beds steady for the first time since the cradle night. Six families from Green Pine Hill have asked to join the clan, two of them with sons who might have a little Qi. We have not said yes to anyone. Qinghe wants to see them first."

"I want to see them eat," says his mother. "A family that does not share its bread will not share anything else."

"Hu is training the guards in the yard behind the forge. Eleven now. Four are close to the first stage." Wenyuan's mouth quirks. "Hu says that if he had known how much work a clan was, he would have stayed one-armed and hated everyone."

"And Feng?"

Feng, at the end of the bench, does not look up. "Fine."

"He is not fine," says Qinghe. "He has been at the pill threshold for a month. He sits in the cave on Terrace Four, and the Qi comes up to the door and will not go through."

"It will."

"It will not unless someone gives you the right pill, and the right pill costs four hundred stones."

"I know the price, Mother."

Jian looks at his brother. Feng is twenty-seven and carries himself like a man of forty. He has shoulders like a door. Something in the set of them makes Jian's stomach turn, because it is the look of a person who has decided not to ask for help.

"I will see to it," Jian says.

"You are in no state—"

"I will see to it, Feng."

His brother's jaw works. Then he nods once, hard, and turns his head so that no one can see his face.

* * *

Zhao Yao finds him in the afternoon.

The boy is fourteen, thin as a lath, with a burn scar over one eyebrow and a quick, careful way of moving that Jian recognizes. It is the way a person walks who has had to keep his feet quiet in a house. He comes in under the Pill Hall's low door with snow on his shoulders, glances at the screen, and then at Bai's back, and waits until the old man has stumped off to the far furnaces before he steps forward.

"Brother Lin."

"Yao. Sit."

"I will not stay long." Zhao Yao does not sit. His voice is flat with the effort of not shaking. "You have been three days gone. I could not come to the stair. They would have asked questions. I only wanted to say that I am glad."

"Thank you."

"And to tell you." He swallows. "My brother. Hui. They have moved him."

Jian sets the bowl down on the cot.

"When?"

"Last week. The steward's letter came to my cousin in the Outer Court. Red Ridge manor, east wing. Not the old rooms by the stable." The boy's fists have closed. "He is seven. He is on a thread. I know it is not my right to ask, because I owe you already for the Wellmaster, and for the stair, and for Lin Yue—"

"Yao."

The boy stops.

"I said that I would get him out," Jian says. "I said it at the Mountain Gate. Did I say it with conditions?"

"No."

"Then there are none." He keeps his voice steady, because the alternative is to let it show how little he has to promise it with. "It will not be tomorrow. I am in no state to cross a courtyard. I will be in the Inner Court by evening, and they will want me still for a month. But I have not forgotten, and you will not have to ask me again."

Zhao Yao looks at him for a long moment. Then he bows, very low, and straightens, and the flatness has gone out of his face. He looks like a boy.

"I will tell my aunt," he says. "She will not believe it."

"Tell her anyway."

He goes out as quietly as he came. Pebble, watching from the pillow, makes a small sound.

Boy, it says. Hui. Soon?

"Not soon," Jian says. "But not never."

* * *

By dusk he is in the Inner Court.

It lies on the shoulder of the mountain above the Outer terraces, behind a second gate of white stone with a plain archway. The buildings are older than the Outer Court's, built of dark timber and gray slate, and the paths between them are swept clean of snow. There is a bell tower. There is a long hall with a pool in front of it, and the pool is frozen over, and under the ice a few orange fish hang as still as leaves.

A steward with a lantern leads him through the cold. He is given a cell. It is a room for one, with a window, a bed with a quilt, a low table, a brazier, and a shelf with three books on it. It is warmer than any room he has had in the Sect. It is also, he understands at once, a cage with good furniture.

His tokens are gone. The Outer Court badge, the gray-green slip with 0417 burned into it, has been taken at the gate and replaced with a white jade tag on a cord, marked with a single character: Gate. His Contribution points are frozen, pending the review. His bunk in the Reed Courtyard, the cooking pots, the corner by the east wall where he mixed powders at night, all of it is struck from the register. He will not be allowed back for a year.

Terrace Nine, he thinks. The boy with the bowl. The cook with the aprons. They were the cover he stood behind. They saw nothing, because he gave them nothing to see. Now the cover is gone, and he stands in a bright room in a strange wing with a tag around his neck, and everyone in the Sect knows his name.

He sits on the bed. The quilt smells of cedar.

"I will sleep," he says to Pebble. "I will sleep for a day."

Sleep, says Pebble. I watch.

He sits on the edge of the bed, and the lamp is still burning, when the knock comes.

* * *

It is soft and exact, and the door opens before he can answer.

She is smaller than he remembered. The Sutra Hall Elder is sixty or perhaps seventy, wrapped in a gray robe with long sleeves, her braid pinned up now in a coil. She carries a lantern in one hand and a scroll case under her arm. Her eyes are a pale, steady brown, and they take in the room, the bed, the cloak, the animal, the boy, in a single sweep, with the economy of a scholar checking a page for errors.

"You may stay seated," she says. "I will not be long."

"Elder."

"The Inner Court has rules." She sets the lantern on the table. "There are forty-one of them, and you will read all forty-one tomorrow, because the steward will bring you a copy. The ones you must know tonight are four. You do not leave the Inner Court without a pass signed by me. You do not enter the Sutra Hall's lower vaults without me. You keep the jade tag on your person, always, because it is how the Gate recognizes you." She lifts one finger for each. "And you tell me, within a day, if anything unusual happens to you."

"Unusual."

"I will leave the word to your judgment. I have found that a man tells you a good deal by what he decides is unusual."

He thinks of the slip of paper he has not yet found, and for an instant the thought almost shows. He sits still. "I understand."

"I doubt it. But you are polite, and that is a beginning." She sits on the stool, uninvited, with her scroll case upright between her knees. For a while she says nothing, and the lantern hisses. "You have been three days inside a Founders' room. Elder Qin tells me you will say nothing of it to the council. I do not intend to ask you to speak of it tonight. I intend to ask you a different question."

"Elder?"

"Did the room have a library?"

He keeps his face blank. "A shelf. A few books."

"One of which you took."

The silence stretches. In his lap, Pebble holds very still.

"A small one," he says at last. "It was lying on a chair. I think it was meant to be kept."

"Ah." Ye nods, slowly, with something like satisfaction. "You do not lie well, Lin Jian. It is a good fault. I will not ask to see the book. I will ask only that you do not burn it, and do not lose it, and do not show it to anyone else until you have shown it to me." She rises. "Not tomorrow. Not this month. When you are ready. I can wait. I have waited a long time for a Founders' book."

"I will do that."

"Good." She takes up the lantern. At the door she pauses with her back to him. "The Sutra Hall has a register older than the Rule. It names the Founder's disciples, and the page that names the last of them has been torn out. I have wanted for forty years to know whose name was on it." Her voice does not change. "When the time comes, I think you will help me. I hope you will not regret it."

The door closes behind her. He sits for a long time in the lamplight, with the sound of her footsteps going away down the corridor, and a feeling like a hand on the back of his neck.

Then he lies down in his tunic, with the cloak over him, and the seed under his ribs turns once in its dark, and he is gone.

* * *

He wakes in the small hours to the sound of nothing.

The brazier has burned low. A single ember glows red in the ash. Outside, the snow has stopped, and the sky through the window is a hard black full of stars. He lies still and lets his senses open slowly, ring by ring, as he has learned to do, and the room settles into shape around him. The table. The shelf. The door.

And on the pillow beside his head, a small white square of paper.

He did not put it there.

Pebble is awake. It is rigid at the foot of the bed, scales flared, and as he looks at it the pangolin makes the thin, high sound that means a seam has closed. Not me, it says. Not door. Not window. Nothing came.

Nothing came, and a slip of paper lies on his pillow, folded once.

He opens it with two fingers. The writing is small and exact, in a clerk's hand, in ink that has not yet dried.

Three days is a long time to be gone. Welcome back, Operator.

There is no signature. There is no seal. In the place where a name should be there is only a blank, and he looks at it and thinks, very clearly, of a line in a small black book.

Beware the ones who wear no names.

He sits up. The Seal gives one hard beat in his chest.

Outside the door, in the corridor, a floorboard creaks, and goes quiet again, as if someone who had been standing there for a long time has just decided to leave.
